title: Instrumentation and form of 'Bloos'
summary: He chose bassoon, contrabassoon, violin and three cellos to collect the essences of blues.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: How did you determine what you wanted to do? The reason I ask that, for posterity is obviously all of us would like to add strings to the standard band and such, but not all of us have an ambition to have two contrabass bassoons, two contra bassoons.
I had a bassoon and a contra bassoon. My string section was one violin and three cellos. Coincidentally with Norman making me this offer, I had been thinking about a

composition dealing with what I felt were many of the blues feelings or forms, many of the essences of blues, and I wanted to put all these things in one composition and it seemed to me in the colors that I saw that I would need the instrumentation that I decided on. It was just a feeling that this three cello sound was important to me and I didn't feel that I needed more than one violin for what I heard, for what I required. That's how it came about.

This is sort of a loaded question, loaded very specifically. In blues there is this inserted moment of the standard ten or twelve bars blues thing which has been criticized as being interruptive of the mood of the piece, to sound terribly erudite.

I didn't feel that way, I felt that it had its place among all the other phases. It was as important to some people, and a great many of them, the only form that they'll accept. They'll scream for the rest of their life if the other parts are not genuine blues.
It's like the people that say baby, it don't swing, how can it be jazz. I can sit quietly and be just as excited as anybody that's moving around.
It was important to me; that's why it was there.
